profile.name: Martin Ignacio Zangl
profile.headline: Senior Android & Mobile Engineer
profile.summary: I build reliable mobile products and developer-facing SDKs across Android, iOS, Flutter, and React Native.
longSummary: I am a senior software engineer with 15+ years of experience building mobile products and developer-facing SDKs for companies including PayPal, MercadoLibre, Checkout.com, and Swift Medical.

My work sits where architecture, product delivery, and reliability meet: modernizing legacy systems without stopping delivery, improving performance on constrained devices, creating strong testing cultures, and keeping behavior consistent across platforms.
I have delivered products across fintech, healthcare, IoT, education, social platforms, and gaming, while mentoring engineers and leading architecture workshops.

work.summary: Delivered React Native SDK work through its Android and iOS dependencies and used merchant-facing sample development to identify platform differences.
achievements: Fixed critical React Native SDK bugs and implemented required Android and iOS changes before completing the wrapper work for release.
Developed the public Android sample using the iOS sample as the agreed design reference.
Documented platform differences and created follow-up tasks.
Prioritized merchant-requested fixes, joined issue discussions, and onboarded a new iOS developer from Parser.
Owned co-branded card-scheme development with open display-priority requirements and took on Gradle configuration tooling for an internal sample.
outcomes: The native dependency changes and completed React Native work were included in a release.
Platform differences were documented for follow-up. Publication of the public sample and resolution of every difference are not claimed.
Card-scheme and configuration-tooling work describe contributions in progress; their shipping and adoption outcomes are not established.

story.title: Following SDK fixes across platform boundaries
story.context: As a Parser contractor on Checkout.com’s Android Payment Flow team, I worked on a public merchant sample and took responsibility for critical React Native SDK bugs and incomplete features.
story.challenge: Completing wrapper features required native releases first. Sample development also exposed differences in configuration, styling, and behavior between Android and iOS.
decisions: Native dependency changes had to be published before the React Native work could be completed. I followed the dependency chain across both native platforms.
Without a UX designer for the merchant sample, my engineering manager and I agreed to use the existing iOS sample as the Android reference.
Co-branded card presentation required an agreed business rule. Display priority remained an open requirement; this work is not presented as shipped payment-routing functionality.
quality: Compared SDK configuration, styling, and behavior while building the sample and working across native platforms.
Recorded inconsistencies as follow-up tasks and used merchant discussions to understand and prioritize stability issues.
Kept internal configuration tooling separate from the public sample: the Gradle approach generated Android resources from multiple API-key sources.

work.summary: Restored stalled document synchronization and improved stability through an application-owned queue, profiling, and incremental modernization.
achievements: Introduced an application-owned database queue and separated connectivity policy from WorkManager scheduling.
Piloted Coroutines in a low-priority synchronization area, compared memory and CPU behavior, then extended the migration.
Profiled document creation and prioritized frequently used flows for a staged migration from RxJava and MVP to Coroutines and MVVM.
Led the replacement of Mixpanel with an internal analytics library and monitored its staged production rollout.
Supported native camera plugins and FHIR data structures in the Flutter product; enabled SwiftVision on ARM64 iOS simulators and migrated native dependencies for 16 KB pages.
outcomes: Documents that had been waiting on customer devices for months successfully synchronized.
The application gained explicit synchronization queue ownership and better processing observability.
SwiftVision shipped with ARM64 iOS Simulator support, and native-library support for 16 KB pages was delivered by the required deadline.

story.title: Making offline clinical work reliable
story.context: Swift Medical’s clinical Android application supported offline document creation and image capture. I later joined the team supporting its production Flutter application, working on native Android and iOS capabilities.
story.challenge: Failed synchronization was the main customer complaint. Pending work was coupled to WorkManager’s internal state, and out-of-order operations were rejected by the backend. Some documents remained on devices for months. Long sessions also exposed memory leaks and expensive bitmap and encryption work.
decisions: The product needed to own synchronization state and ordering. WorkManager remained responsible for scheduling execution, while the application database held pending domain operations.
A measured pilot established whether Coroutines improved the existing thread-heavy implementation before extending the change. Frequently used flows took priority over a wholesale rewrite.

Clean Architecture made replacing analytics practical, but production behavior still determined rollout readiness. I stopped the first limited rollout when results were unacceptable, iterated on the library, and released again.
quality: Used CPU and Memory Profilers, allocation and leak analysis, and Perfetto to investigate long-session failures and blocked threads.
Compared resource use before expanding the synchronization migration and monitored adoption and performance during analytics rollout.
Compiled OpenCV and TensorFlow dependencies for ARM64 iOS simulators and validated SwiftVision with the computer-vision team before its production release.

work.summary: Expanded validation beyond unit tests, traced an incorrect balance to its business rule, and owned module integration across release trains.
achievements: Mapped the Savings journey and documented existing behavior before planning small refactors.
Introduced integration and end-to-end validation alongside existing unit tests.
Built a test library to inject and queue backend responses, including edge cases, with Page Objects for reusable customer journeys.
Restructured functional flows with MVVM and unidirectional data flow and worked with DevOps on Jenkins coverage reporting.
Owned module release integration and coordinated fixes for cross-module conflicts.
outcomes: Exposed and reproduced an incorrect balance that previously required a manual refresh, protecting corrected behavior with automation.
Established reusable scenarios for full financial journeys.
Resolved a cross-module theme conflict before it delayed feature integration.

story.title: Making financial journeys reproducible
story.context: I joined PayPal Savings while it was an MVP in production. Its customer journey covered compliance, activation, balance operations, and funding sources. I later moved to Credits UK, contributing across Android, iOS, and Java backend work.
story.challenge: Strong unit coverage did not establish that complete customer journeys worked across module, API, and UI boundaries. One business-rule defect displayed an incorrect balance until the customer refreshed.
decisions: Incremental refactoring preserved verified behavior in a live financial product while allowing delivery to continue.

Explicit event-to-state paths made asynchronous compliance, funding, and balance operations easier to trace. Reproducible backend responses connected a visible balance inconsistency to the underlying business rule.
End-to-end tests broadened confidence but cost more to maintain. Queued responses and Page Objects controlled environment variability and repetitive setup.
quality: Measured coverage across unit, integration, and end-to-end layers in Jenkins.
Reproduced success and failure scenarios with controlled backend responses and verified corrected balance behavior.
Tested the assembled application in release trains. During a theme migration, traced a duplicate dependency to another module and coordinated the correction.

work.summary: Built shared resources and virtual credit-card flows, connecting API contracts, reusable components, customer journeys, and application observability.
achievements: Built a small resource-handling SDK for shared assets.
Helped define mobile and middle-end contracts for screen payloads and customer interaction events, contributing middle-end changes when needed.
Created and registered UI components, documented complex behavior, and prepared components for shared use when reuse justified it.
Used FLEX dispatchers and stores for complex server-driven flows with explicit state and event paths.
Defined engineering and product metrics and collaborated with the architecture team on application-wide observability.
outcomes: Delivered resource handling and components intended for consumption across product teams.
Connected mobile payloads, customer events, and telemetry within complete product flows.
Identified release-train edge cases and worked with the architecture team on observability improvements.

story.title: Connecting feature ownership to platform reliability
story.context: At MercadoLibre, product teams owned modules within a larger application and contributed to common libraries. I worked on virtual credit-card flows and shared resources, including integrations with Andes UI Components and Andes Images.
story.challenge: A feature had to fit a platform used by many teams. Contracts, UI behavior, edge cases, and telemetry needed to stay coherent when modules came together in release trains.
decisions: Feature-specific behavior stayed in its owning module. Shared components needed a clear reuse case because API evolution, compatibility, and governance affected other teams.
Server-driven composition supported flows that benefited from middle-end control. FLEX made state transitions explicit without requiring every screen to become dynamic.
Module autonomy made release-train validation essential. Integration edge cases became inputs to shared observability improvements.
quality: Tested module behavior and edge cases against required coverage expectations.
Defined latency percentiles from P50 through P99 alongside customer-journey progression and payment timing signals.
Investigated alerts and weak product metrics with the team, sharing discoveries and clarifying initially incomplete use cases.
